source_refs.note: Unnumbered topic Functional Group Interconversion as printed, with Quick Check 25.1 (PDF 136-137); Figures 25.3 and 25.4 are redrawn.

blocks.text: FGI is a phenomenon to change a functional group into another functional group, required for synthesis of a specific of compound. FGI has a crucial role to play in designing routes which lead to target molecules. Simple starting materials can be converted to more complex target molecules using FGI as building blocks. FGI not only allows to create the carbon skeleton of the target molecule but also select the route to be adopted for this purpose.
The interconversions of functional groups have been studied in detail in earlier chapters and a summary of these interconversions is given in Figure 25.3 and 25.4.

blocks.alt: Map of interconversions between two-carbon compounds: alkene H2C=CH2, halogenoalkane CH3-CH2-Br, amine CH3-CH2-NH2, aldehyde, alcohol CH3-CH2-OH, amide, ester, carboxylic acid and acid halide, with reagents on the arrows: HBr, KOH (alcohol), NH3, Heat/H2SO4, H2O/H2SO4, PBr3, KOH (aq), K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, NaBH4, V2O5, LiAlH4, C2H5OH/H+, SOCl2.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.3: Functional group interconversion in aliphatic organic compounds (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 25.3 has an arrow labelled NH₃ from ethanol to ethanamide; ammonia does not convert an alcohol into an amide, so this arrow is left out.

blocks.alt: Benzene in the centre: CH3Cl/AlCl3 up to toluene; SO3/H2SO4 left to benzene sulfonic acid, then (i) NaOH (ii) HCl down to phenol; HNO3/H2SO4 right to nitrobenzene, then Sn, HCl down to aniline; ethanoyl chloride/AlCl3 down to acetophenone. Toluene gives benzyl alcohol with (i) Cl2, light (ii) KOH(aq) and benzoic acid with KMnO4/H2SO4.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.4: Functional group interconversion in aromatic organic compounds (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed label “benene sulfonic acid” is misspelt; it is benzene sulfonic acid.
